Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right! Woman! too long degraded, scorned, opprest; O born to rule in partial Law's despite, Resume thy native empire o'er the breast! Go forth arrayed in panoply divine; That angel pureness which admits no stain; Go, bid proud Man his boasted rule resign, And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign. Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store Of bright artillery glancing from afar; Soft melting tones thy thundering cannon's roar, Blushes and fears thy magazine of war. Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim,— Felt, not defined, and if debated, lost; Like sacred mysteries, which withheld from fame, Shunning discussion, are revered the most. Try all that wit and art suggest to bend Of thy imperial foe the stubborn knee; Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend; Thou mayst command, but never canst be free. Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude; Soften the sullen, clear the cloudy brow: Be, more than princes' gifts, thy favours sued;— She hazards all, who will the least allow. But hope not, courted idol of mankind, On this proud eminence secure to stay; Subduing and subdued, thou soon shalt find Thy coldness soften, and thy pride give way. Then, then, abandon each ambitious thought, Conquest or rule thy heart shall feebly move, In Nature's school, by her soft maxims taught, That separate rights are lost in mutual love.

Indeed, wounded Woman, stand up and claim what belongs to you! For far too long you have been humiliated, mocked, and held down. You were meant to govern, regardless of what one-sided laws declare, so take back the natural authority you hold over the human heart.

Step forward clothed in sacred armor—that flawless, angelic purity that no blemish can touch. Command arrogant Man to give up the power he brags about, and let him bow to kiss the golden staff of your rule.

Prepare yourself with charm as your weapon; gather your arsenal of dazzling ammunition that shines from a distance. Let gentle, tender voices serve as your booming cannon fire, and let blushes and timid glances be your stockpile of weaponry.

Your entitlement is complete dominion—demand nothing lesser than that. Such power is something felt rather than spelled out, and once it becomes a subject of argument, it disappears. It is like holy secrets that gain the most reverence precisely because they are kept hidden and never opened to debate.

Attempt every clever trick and skill you can imagine to force your royal enemy to his knees. Turn deceitful Man into someone you rule over rather than a companion; you may issue orders, yet you will never truly be at liberty.

Intimidate those who would take liberties, and hold back the crude. Ease the moody, and smooth away a frowning face. Let your kindnesses be begged for as though they outweigh the presents of royalty—for any woman who grants even a little puts everything at risk.

But do not expect, you cherished idol whom all pursue, that you can rest safely on this lofty height. Both the one who conquers and the one conquered, you will soon discover that your indifference melts and your pride surrenders.

At that moment, let go of every ambitious desire; the wish to dominate or command will barely stir your heart. Instructed in Nature's classroom by her gentle lessons, you will learn that individual claims of right dissolve away within shared, mutual love.

# On Women's Power and the Path to True Freedom

The poem issues a stirring call to women, urging them to rise up and reclaim a natural power and influence that has long lain dormant, suppressed for generations by unequal laws and the rigid conventions of society. It presents this reclamation not as the seizing of something foreign, but as the recovery of something that has always rightfully belonged to women—a birthright buried beneath centuries of injustice.

In pursuit of this aim, the poem encourages women to make use of their distinctly feminine qualities. Purity, charm, grace, and emotional appeal are cast as instruments of influence—weapons, even—through which women might gain a measure of dominion over men. Rather than competing on the terms set by men, women are counseled to draw upon their own particular strengths to establish their sway.

The speaker further advises that this power is most effective when it remains undefined and unspoken. Its potency lies precisely in its subtlety; to expose it to open debate or discussion would be to weaken rather than fortify it. What is left implicit retains its mystery and force, while what is dragged into the light of argument loses its quiet command.

Yet the poem does not offer this vision without qualification. It cautions that such dominance over men is inherently unstable and can never amount to genuine freedom. To command another is not the same as to be free oneself; a power built upon manipulation and mastery carries within it the seeds of its own fragility, and it binds the ruler as surely as the ruled.

In its final movement, the poem arrives at a more profound conclusion. It urges women to abandon altogether the ambitions of conquest and rule, and to embrace in their place the ideal of mutual love. In such a union, the notion of separate and competing rights dissolves entirely, giving way to a shared partnership in which neither party seeks to dominate the other. True freedom, the poem suggests, is found not in ruling but in loving—not in power over another, but in union with them.

# The Rights of Woman: Barbauld's Ironic Vision of Female Power

Anna Laetitia Barbauld's poem "The Rights of Woman" engages directly with one of the most contentious debates of the late eighteenth century: the question of women's power and their proper place in society. Written during a period of intense discussion about the natural rights of individuals—debates spurred by revolutionary movements and by pioneering feminist works such as Mary Wollstonecraft's "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman"—Barbauld's poem takes an unexpected approach to the subject. Rather than advocating for legal or political equality, the poem adopts an ironic stance, exhorting women to seek dominion over men through the very qualities traditionally associated with femininity.

## The Call to "Empire"

The poem opens with a stirring, almost militant summons for woman to "rise" and assert her injured rights. Yet the power Barbauld describes is not the power of citizenship, education, or legal standing. Instead, she urges women to wield their influence through emotional manipulation, charm, and the careful deployment of feminine wiles. Woman is encouraged to conquer through beauty, blushes, and the softness of her nature—to establish an "empire" over the hearts of men. In this vision, feminine power operates not through reasoned argument or institutional reform but through the subtle arts of persuasion and allure, transforming traditional markers of female weakness into instruments of control.

## The Ironic Undercutting

However, Barbauld does not allow this vision of feminine conquest to stand unchallenged. As the poem progresses, its rhetoric of triumph begins to collapse under the weight of its own contradictions. The poet reveals that an empire built upon manipulation and adversarial struggle can only lead to isolation and estrangement. Power won through calculation and emotional gamesmanship, she suggests, offers no true fulfillment—it produces a hollow sovereignty that separates women from genuine human connection. The very pursuit of dominance over men, whether through legal rights or through feminine wiles, is shown to be a fundamentally flawed enterprise, one that mistakes conquest for liberation.

## Mutual Love as Resolution

In its concluding movement, the poem proposes an alternative to the entire framework of competing rights and gendered warfare. Rather than positioning men and women as adversaries locked in a contest for supremacy, Barbauld advocates for the mutual abandonment of separate claims to power. Both sexes, she suggests, should relinquish their assertions of dominance in favor of reciprocal love and shared understanding. The true resolution to the "rights of woman" question lies not in one gender triumphing over the other, but in a harmonious partnership grounded in affection and mutual respect—a state in which the very language of rights and empire becomes irrelevant.

## Cultural Tensions

This resolution reflects the complex and often ambivalent attitudes of Barbauld's era toward women's social role. The poem simultaneously acknowledges the legitimate grievances that fuel demands for women's rights while expressing deep skepticism about power itself as a solution. Barbauld's refusal to endorse either traditional feminine submission or outright feminist assertion reveals the difficult position occupied by thoughtful women of her time, who recognized the injustices they faced yet remained uncertain about the remedies. In this way, "The Rights of Woman" stands as a nuanced meditation on gender, power, and the possibility of equality—one that resists easy conclusions and instead captures the profound tensions surrounding women's place in the changing social landscape of the late eighteenth century.

# Yes: Women and the Law

## A Journey Toward Equality

The word "Yes" carries profound significance in the history of women's relationship with the law. It represents the affirmative victories won through generations of struggle, advocacy, and perseverance.

### Historical Milestones

For much of history, the answer to women's rights was "No." Could a woman vote? No. Could she own property independently? No. Could she pursue higher education or enter certain professions? Often, no.

The transformation of these answers into "Yes" marks some of the most important social progress in modern civilization:

- **Yes**, women can vote (achieved in various nations throughout the 20th century)
- **Yes**, women can own and inherit property
- **Yes**, women can hold public office
- **Yes**, women can access equal education
- **Yes**, women deserve equal pay for equal work

### The Ongoing Work

While legal frameworks in many countries now affirm women's equality, the gap between law on paper and law in practice remains a challenge worldwide. Legislation provides the foundation, but true equality requires:

1. **Enforcement** of existing protections
2. **Cultural change** alongside legal reform
3. **Access to justice** for all women, regardless of circumstance
4. **Representation** of women in legal and political institutions

### Conclusion

The story of women and law is ultimately a story of expanding human dignity. Each "Yes" represents not just a legal victory, but a recognition of fundamental human worth.

---

**To Woman**

Awake, O Woman, from thy patient sleep,
Too long hast thou consented, still, to weep;
Too long hast bowed thy proud, unconquered head,
And begged for crumbs where thou shouldst break the bread.
Arise, and take the sceptre none should hold
By right of muscle, or by right of gold;
Thy mind is keen, thy spirit swift and whole,
No lesser lamp was kindled in thy soul.
Reclaim the voice they taught thee to suppress,
The name, the wage, the world, the very dress;
Stand equal in the council and the hall,

And let thy judgment carry equal sway.
Demand thy portion of the common light—
Not favor granted, but thy sovereign right.

And justice reigns where once oppression rose,
Look then on him who marches at thy side,
No more thy master, and no more thy pride
In conquest—for the war was never won
To leave two nations where God meant but one.
For love, that older law, absolves the claim
Of "mine" and "thine," and blends them in one flame;
Two rights, contending, sink beneath its art,
And rise, made single, in a single heart.
Not thou o'er him, nor he above thee set,
But each in each, the separate selves forget;
Where love has entered, boundaries efface—
Not rival thrones, but one abiding grace.

## The Colonial Lover's Argument

*I.*
You speak of conquest as a lover's art,
Of nations won as maidens might be wooed,
Yet I have watched the taking break the heart
Of those whose only crime was solitude.
The banner planted on the foreign shore
Casts shadows where the tender grasses grew;
You call it glory—I have named it war,
And weep for all the world your hands undo.

*II.*
"But woman's province is the hearth," you cry,
"Not politics of empire, sword, or throne."
As if my sex could bind my reasoning eye,
Or make the pain of others less my own!
The chains you forge for peoples far away
Are wrought in the same fire that fashions mine;
The subject and the wife, in their dismay,
Both learn to call obedience "divine."

Yet love I do—and here confess it plain:
Not love that kneels, but love that dares to stand,
That would not see you master, nor me chain,
But walk as equals through this troubled land.
Come, lay your empire and your pride to rest;
The only realm worth ruling is the heart,
And that domain is governed, at its best,
Where neither reigns, and neither dwells apart.

---

- **Gender**: The speaker challenges the confinement of women to domestic "provinces"
